text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive the interface dispersion relation from kinematic and pressure conditions, estimate growth from Atwood number and wavelength, and identify the linear regime. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Denser fluid above can lower its potential energy Denser fluid below lighter fluid is a stable arrangement under gravity. If the denser fluid is above, a small downward deformation lets dense fluid sink while lighter fluid rises. Releasing potential energy amplifies the deformation: Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Take z upward and acceleration −g with g > 0. The upper and lower half-spaces have constant densities ρ₁ and ρ₂. Both are infinitely deep, incompressible, and inviscid, with no surface tension, magnetic field, or background flow. Unlike Jeans instability, we prescribe g rather than calculate perturbed self-gravity. ζ(x,t) = Re[ζ₀ei(kx−ωt)], k = 2πλ > 0 ζ is interface height. Complex exponentials are a calculational tool; the physical displacement is the real part. For ω = ωr + iσ, e−iωt = e−iωrteσt, so σ > 0 means growth. Linearization requires k|ζ| ≪ 1. 02Build a flow that decays away from the interface In each fluid take potential perturbations δu = ∇φ. Incompressibility, ∇·δu = 0, gives ∇²φ = 0. With x dependence eikx, the vertical equation is φ″ − k²φ = 0. Choose solutions that decay far from the interface. φ₁ = a₁e−kzei(kx−ωt) (z > 0) φ₂ = a₂ekzei(kx−ωt) (z < 0) The interface moves with the fluid, so its vertical speed ∂ζ/∂t equals ∂φ/∂z on either side. At first order evaluate at z = 0. Removing the common exponential gives: −iωζ₀ = −ka₁ = ka₂ a₁ = iωζ₀k, a₂ = −iωζ₀k 03Keep the background pressure gradient Spatial integration of linearized momentum gives δpj = −ρj∂φj/∂t = iρjωφj. Pressures match at the displaced interface z = ζ. The equilibrium gradient dp₀/dz = −ρg adds a term −ρgζ when evaluating there. δp₁−ρ₁gζ = δp₂−ρ₂gζ δp₁−δp₂ = (ρ₁−ρ₂)gζ The amplitudes above give δp₁ = −ρ₁ω²ζ₀/k and δp₂ = +ρ₂ω²ζ₀/k. Subtract them and cancel nonzero ζ₀. −(ρ₁+ρ₂)ω²k = (ρ₁−ρ₂)g ω² = −Agk, A ≡ ρ₁−ρ₂ρ₁+ρ₂ A is the Atwood number. Denser fluid on top gives A > 0 and ω = ±i√(Agk); the growing branch has σ = √(Agk). If A < 0, ω is real and the interface supports gravity waves in this model. τgrow = 1σ = √(λ2πAg) (A > 0) 04Explore density contrast and wavelength Multiplying both densities by the same factor leaves A unchanged. Reducing wavelength by four increases k by four and growth rate by two. The doubling time is ln2/σ; 1/σ is the e-folding time. With A = 0 and no shear, this ideal interface has neither restoring force nor growth. 05Separate linear growth from nonlinear mixing This calculation describes only the small-amplitude stage. Large bubbles, dense spikes, and entrainment require nonlinear dynamics. At contacts in supernova remnants, examine density ordering relative to the effective acceleration in a frame following the decelerating flow. Without surface tension, viscosity, magnetic effects, or finite interface thickness, σ ∝ √k has no finite fastest-growing wavelength. If a numerical result changes with resolution, check the physical small-scale regulator and the prescribed initial perturbations. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Let the top fluid have three times the bottom density, downward g = 1 m/s², and wavelength λ = 2π m. What are the growth rate and e-folding time? What if the fluids are exchanged? Show the answer and reasoning A = (3−1)/(3+1) = 1/2 and k = 1 m⁻¹. Thus σ = 1/√2 s⁻¹ and the e-folding time is √2 s. Swapping the fluids makes A = −1/2, giving positive ω² = gk/2: oscillation instead of exponential growth in this idealization.
